metadata.title: Tropical forest biomass vulnerability (TFVI), 0.1-degree grid
metadata.description: Tropical Forest Vulnerability Index for above-ground biomass, supplied with Saatchi et al. (2021). Negative values indicate vulnerability toward sustained biomass loss; positive values indicate vulnerability toward higher biomass. Values near zero indicate relative stability. This is a modeled, standardized index, not a biomass stock map or a probability.
metadata.citation: Saatchi et al. (2021). Supporting scripts for 'Detecting Vulnerability of Humid Tropical Forests to Multiple Stressors'. Zenodo. https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.5115158
metadata.study_time: Above-ground biomass response observations: 2000-2018. Broader study and long-term stressor records: 1982-2018.

publications.title: Detecting vulnerability of humid tropical forests to multiple stressors
publications.citation: Saatchi, S., et al. (2021). Detecting vulnerability of humid tropical forests to multiple stressors. One Earth 4(7), 988-1003. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.oneear.2021.06.002

annotations.preparation_status: Prepared and checked for the EOLab pilot; scientific limitations remain.
limitations: This pilot preserves the published pan-tropical grid; it is not an Amazon-only subset.
The native file contains substantial negative and positive extremes. These must not be clipped, converted to percentages or interpreted as probabilities.
The 0.1-degree source is not the 0.25-degree visualization shown in the main paper. A second 0.1-degree file in FigureS11 is an exact duplicate and should not become a second dataset.
The paper treats the findings as correlational. The model assumes stationary sensitivities and resilience and does not estimate societal impacts.
The paper specifically notes weaker consistency between AGB vulnerability and variance patterns, potentially related to shorter/annual biomass records.
The scientific analysis was not rerun. Format conversion verifies data preservation, not the correctness of the study model.
Exact map observation dates are not embedded. Preserve documented input/study periods separately and label any file-modification temporal fallback.

source_sheet_rows.study_location: the entire Amazon basin, including regions from Bolivia, Brazil, Colombia, Ecuador, Guyana, and Peru

source_sheet_rows.dataset_description: Climatic-environmental suitability and presence-absence potential distribution of 52 frugivorous fish species of socioeconomic value, projected on the hydrographic network of the Amazon River basin for both the present and the future under two climatic scenarios (moderate: SSP2-4.5 and pessimistic: SSP5-8.5).

source_sheet_annotations.dataset_description: Mean ranking of reservoir impact for individual current and future barriers, considering their potential for hydrological fragmentation and blocking access to climate refuge areas for fish, obtained from the leave-one-out barrier prioritization simulation (dCCI) across climate scenarios and fish groups.
source_sheet_annotations.relationship_description: The distribution of the species was modeled as a function of bioclimatic and hydrological variables (Table S4) covering the Amazon hydrographic network.

source_sheet_rows.title: Reduced Vegetation Uptake During the Extreme 2023 Drought Turns the Amazon Into a Weak Carbon Source
source_sheet_rows.study_objective: Here, we evaluate the response of the Amazon carbon cycle to this extreme event across different spatial scales.
source_sheet_rows.existing_data_description: ERA5 reanalysis data and ERA5-Land; MSWEP V2.8; GLEAM v4.2a; the GFAS and GFED4s satellite-based global fire emission products; the OCO2-Inv satellite-driven atmospheric inversion; TROPOMI SIF and OCO2-SIF; MODIS BRDF-corrected surface reflectance (MCD43C4v061); L-band vegetation optical depth (L-VOD); GRACE data for the Amazon basin.
source_sheet_rows.relationship_description: Strong negative correlations between spatial anomalies in GPP and VPD (r = -0.69, p < 0.001), a moderate but significant negative correlation between TER and temperature anomalies (r = -0.48, p < 0.001), and significant negative correlations of both GPP (r = -0.58, p < 0.001) and TER (r = -0.55, p < 0.001) with CWD.
source_sheet_rows.dataset_description: The monthly totals of NEE, GPP and Reco at ATTO, obtained from filtered high-quality half-hourly turbulent eddy covariance CO2 fluxes measured at 81 m above ground level, with gap-filling and EC-NEE partitioning to Gross Primary Productivity (GPP) and Ecosystem Respiration (Reco)
source_sheet_rows.download_source: All the processed data integrated for the biogeographic Amazon area can be found here: https://doi.org/10.17617/3.OU3KYA (Botia et al., 2026). Additionally, on the same repository, the monthly totals of NEE, GPP and Reco at ATTO, together with the monthly mean delta CO2 can be also found in tabular form.
